target: AG1’s claim that AI is good for society because it improves convenience, health, accessibility, safety, and productivity
objection: AI’s apparent benefits overlook major harms that routinely accompany deployment, including worker displacement, weaker critical thinking, biased outcomes, privacy invasion, and surveillance creep. In AG2’s view, those harms mean AI is harmful overall rather than broadly beneficial.

target: AG1’s assumption that automation mainly saves time and helps workers and students
objection: Automating routine tasks often replaces workers, depresses wages, and shifts employment toward fragile gig-style work; even if productivity rises, the gains are not shared evenly and can reduce bargaining power and stability.

target: AG1’s claim that AI helps students and professionals by assisting with learning
objection: AI assistance can become overreliance, causing people to outsource evaluation and reasoning to fluent outputs. That weakens the ability to check sources, spot errors, and think independently.

target: AG1’s claim that AI can expand accessibility and help marginalized groups
objection: AI systems trained on biased data can reproduce and amplify discrimination in areas like hiring, policing, lending, and personalization, so the same tools that help some users can also exclude or misclassify marginalized people.

target: AG1’s claim that AI can be implemented responsibly to protect privacy
objection: Responsible implementation is not a guarantee because AI often depends on large-scale collection of sensitive data such as text, voice, images, location, and behavior patterns, and business incentives push toward data harvesting and surveillance.

target: AG1’s claim that AI can improve workplace safety through monitoring risks
objection: Safety monitoring can quickly become broader worker surveillance that discourages reporting and increases stress, especially when oversight and accountability are weak.

target: AG1’s view that the harms of AI are merely engineering or policy problems that can be mitigated
objection: In practice, safeguards often fail because companies have incentives to collect more data, deploy faster, and maximize engagement or productivity, while regulations lag behind rapidly changing models and uses.

target: AG1’s claim that fairness audits, bias reduction, and privacy-preserving techniques can make AI safe enough
objection: Bias and privacy trade-offs are not clean: mitigation often requires resources and can reduce performance, so organizations under competitive pressure tend to choose utility and scale over full protection, leaving residual bias and data collection in place.

target: AG1’s claim that workplace safety monitoring can be limited to specific, accountable uses
objection: In real deployments, narrow safety metrics tend to expand into productivity tracking, behavioral prediction, and discipline. Without strong worker control, surveillance predictably grows beyond its original purpose.

target: AG1’s conclusion that AI can be net good if harms are managed
objection: Governance and enforcement are hard to sustain at scale because regulators often lack technical capacity, resources, and real-time access to proprietary systems, so the gap between policy and actual deployment undermines the net-good case.

target: AG1’s assumption that liability, audit logs, and remedies can shift enforceability onto companies
objection: Those tools depend on transparency that vendors often will not provide, and many AI harms are hard to detect, prove, or reverse, so enforcement can become superficial rather than meaningful.

target: AG1’s claim that AI does not necessarily concentrate power
objection: AI tends to concentrate power in large firms that control data, compute, distribution, and model IP, and smaller organizations face heavier compliance costs and weaker infrastructure, which harms competition and economic resilience.

target: AG1’s selective-deployment argument that AI can be good if high-risk uses are restricted and low-risk uses are allowed
objection: Even so-called low-risk uses still create privacy and bias harms at scale, and products commonly drift from benign convenience tools into high-impact decision-making or tracking systems over time.

target: AG1’s claim that human-in-the-loop and verification prompts can prevent overreliance
objection: Verification prompts do not restore real critical thinking for most users, because many people are time-pressured or lack the expertise to judge the quality of citations and evidence, so they still offload thinking to the AI.

target: AG1’s idea that deployment gates, licensing, and hard technical controls can keep AI bounded over time
objection: Those controls are undermined by model drift, updates, integrations, and downstream misuse; systems that were initially lower risk can become higher risk later, and enforcement is difficult once AI is embedded in products and workflows.

target: AG1’s argument that lifecycle governance, versioning, regression tests, and rollback can keep AI safe enough to be socially beneficial
objection: Rollback cannot reliably undo harms like privacy leaks, biased hiring or lending outcomes, or wrongly denied services, and the compliance burden of such governance favors large firms, deepening power concentration rather than producing a broad social good.

target: AG1’s claim that AI can still be good overall because better governance can improve expected outcomes
objection: Even when controls exist, they either fail to reverse harms or shift the costs of control onto society in ways that concentrate power. Therefore, the recurring real-world harms remain more reliable than the promised benefits, so AI is not good for society overall.
